case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA) requires the federal government to pay tribes contract support costs (CSCs) on healthcare programs funded not only by the Secretarial amount under the ISDEAA contract but also by the tribe’s third‑party revenue (e.g., Medicaid/Medicare/insurance collections) used to operate those contracted programs.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA), primarily 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2)-(3) (definition and payment of “contract support costs”), and related ISDEAA provisions including 25 U.S.C. § 5325(m)(2) (program income not used to reduce contract funding) and 25 U.S.C. § 5329(c) (liberal construction/model agreement clause, as discussed via Ramah).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The federal government (HHS/IHS) argues that CSCs are limited to the costs of administering and supporting the ISDEAA contract as funded by the Secretarial amount, and do not extend to additional work generated by the tribe’s spending of third‑party collections. In the government’s view, tying CSCs to third‑party revenue would improperly expand the government’s payment obligation beyond what Congress appropriated for the contract, conflict with ISDEAA’s program-income rule (that such income cannot reduce the Secretarial amount, but also should not implicitly increase CSC obligations), and create an open-ended, self-amplifying payment duty driven by a tribe’s ability to generate and expend third‑party reimbursements.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The tribes (San Carlos Apache and Northern Arapaho) argue that the text of § 5325(a)(2)-(3) defines CSCs broadly as the reasonable costs required to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of the contracted programs, without limiting those costs to activities funded solely by the Secretarial amount. Because third‑party revenues are used to operate and expand the same contracted health programs, the associated administrative/support costs are still ‘contract support costs’ that the statute requires the Secretary to pay. They contend the government’s reading adds a limitation Congress did not write, is inconsistent with ISDEAA’s pro-tribal interpretive directive (liberal construction), and would undercut tribal self-determination by leaving tribes to absorb necessary overhead costs triggered by delivering services and collecting third‑party reimbursements.
key_precedents: Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, 567 U.S. 182 (2012)
Ali v. Federal Bureau of Prisons, 552 U.S. 214 (2008)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability/open-ended-liability concern is the strongest point for Petitioner, but it ultimately depends on importing a Secretarial-amount-only limiter that the text of § 5325(a)(2)–(3) does not supply. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statute already cabins recovery to costs that are “reasonable” and “required” for contract compliance and prudent management of “the program,” and ordinary cost principles/audit controls give that standard workable content without rewriting “program” to mean “only the Secretarially funded slice.” Ramah is relevant not because it resolves this precise antecedent question, but because (as Justice Thomas notes) it instructs that we should not judicially graft fiscal-control limitations onto ISDEAA payment obligations absent a restriction “clearly required by the statutory language.” Consistent with minimalism and institutional legitimacy, I would hold only that when third-party collections are used to carry out the same contracted program, associated reasonable support costs fall within § 5325(a)(2)–(3), reserving harder cases about unrelated expansions for later.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that tying CSCs to third-party revenue creates an “open-ended” federal obligation—raises a real administrability concern, but it cannot justify inserting a Secretarial-amount cap that the enacted text does not contain. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5325(a)(2)–(3) defines CSCs functionally as the “reasonable costs” of activities the tribe “must” perform to ensure compliance and prudent management of “the program,” and nothing in those words turns on the funding source for services delivered under that program. Nor does § 5325(m)(2) supply Alito’s limitation; as Justice Barrett notes, it is an anti-offset rule, and reading a hidden funding-source ceiling into CSCs would effectively accomplish the very reduction Congress prohibited. Ramah’s instruction that courts not rewrite ISDEAA payment obligations absent a limitation “clearly required” by statutory language reinforces that the reasonableness/necessity constraints—not an atextual Secretarial-amount tether—are the proper textual limits here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that § 5325(a)(2)–(3) contains no express funding-source limitation, but that does not answer the antecedent textual question: what “the program” is for which CSCs are “required” to ensure compliance and “prudent management.” Their approach risks treating “the program” as whatever operational scale a tribe chooses to undertake using third-party revenues, effectively converting a defined contract-support obligation into an expanding federal backstop without a clear statutory anchor, and the “reasonableness” standard alone is too indeterminate to supply that limiting principle. Nor does § 5325(m)(2) (as Justice Thomas reads it) affirmatively expand the CSC base; it is best understood as an anti-offset rule preventing the Government from netting program income against the contract amount, not as a command to make the United States pay incremental administrative costs driven by non-Secretarial funds. Ramah’s “clearly required” language counsels against judicially created prorating or underpayment defenses, but it does not compel enlarging the category of federally payable CSCs beyond costs necessary to carry out the Secretarially funded contract requirements.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s “open-ended, self-amplifying” liability concern presses hard, but it depends on reading “the program” as only the Secretarial-amount-funded slice—an atextual limit that the statute does not supply. As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, § 5325(a)(2)–(3) already cabins recovery to “reasonable” costs that a tribe “must” incur for contract compliance and prudent management, and that standard—applied through ordinary cost principles and audits—directly answers administrability without rewriting the statute. Section 5325(m)(2)’s anti-offset rule reinforces that Congress did not want third-party revenues used to reduce federal obligations; denying CSCs needed to administer those revenues would effectively force tribes to subsidize federally required overhead, with predictable harm to tribal health systems. Under Ramah, highlighted by Justice Gorsuch, the Government has not shown its funding-source cap is “clearly required” by the text, and policy fears about appropriations cannot justify shifting burdens onto tribes absent that clarity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point is the best pushback: if “the program” expands with third-party collections, CSC exposure could look unbounded. But that concern doesn’t supply the missing textual hook—§ 5325(a)(2)–(3) already limits payment to “reasonable costs” for activities the tribe “must” perform to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of the contracted program, and those constraints (plus ordinary cost principles) prevent the self-amplifying, elective expansion Alito fears. Chief Justice Roberts’s reading of § 5325(m)(2) as an anti-offset rule is also important: treating it as an implicit cap would effectively reintroduce netting-out through the back door by forcing tribes to absorb overhead tied to program income used to run the same contracted program. Under Ramah (as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett emphasize), the Government must show its narrowing construction is clearly required by the statutory language, and a Secretarial-amount-only limitation is not.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s “open-ended obligation” point is serious, but it depends on importing a funding-source limitation—“the program” meaning only the Secretarial-amount-funded slice—that the enacted text does not contain. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas note, § 5325(a)(2)–(3) defines reimbursable contract support costs functionally: “reasonable costs” for activities the tribe “must” undertake to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of “the program,” and those obligations can persist even when services are financed in part through third-party collections. Justice Kagan’s reading of § 5325(m)(2) as an anti-offset rule reinforces that Congress did not mean program income to indirectly shrink the federal obligation by forcing tribes to absorb otherwise-required administrative overhead. Under Ramah’s instruction (and the liberal-construction rule in § 5329(c)), I do not see a narrowing construction “clearly required by the statutory language,” so fiscal/administrability concerns cannot justify rewriting the payment duty.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability/open-ended-liability concern is the strongest point for Petitioner, but under the statute Congress wrote, the limiting principle is not the funding source; it is whether the claimed amounts are the “reasonable costs” of activities the tribe “must” perform to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of “the program.” As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, importing a Secretarial-amount-only ceiling would be an atextual rewrite that effectively narrows “the program” to a funding stream rather than the contracted operation, and it would functionally recreate the very sort of underpayment Ramah cautioned against absent a limitation “clearly required” by the text. I agree with Justice Kagan that § 5325(m)(2) reads as an anti-offset rule, and while it is not an affirmative expansion provision, it undercuts any interpretation that forces tribes to internalize federally required overhead simply because program income is involved. Given the statutory reasonableness/necessity constraints and ordinary auditing tools, I do not see a textual hook sufficient to adopt Alito’s cap, so I remain with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest contention—that tying CSCs to third-party revenue creates an “open-ended” federal obligation—highlights a real administrability concern, but it does not supply the textual anchor his reading requires. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5325(a)(2)–(3) defines CSCs by function (reasonable costs a tribe must incur for contract compliance and prudent management of the program), not by funding source, and § 5325(m)(2)’s anti-offset rule cuts against constructions that effectively shift unavoidable overhead to tribes when program income is used to run the same contracted program. Under Ramah’s instruction that limitations must be “clearly required by the statutory language,” I do not see a basis to import a Secretarial-amount-only ceiling; the statute’s own “reasonable costs” constraint is the limiting principle Congress enacted. Administrability and fiscal-control worries are better handled through reasonableness review and ordinary cost principles than by judicially rewriting the payment obligation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s open-ended-liability concern is the most serious counterweight, but I do not see a textual basis in § 5325(a)(2)–(3) for the funding-source cap he proposes; those provisions ask whether the tribe must incur “reasonable” support costs to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of the contracted program as it is actually administered. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, that reasonableness/necessity framework—plus ordinary audit and contract-cost principles—provides a workable limiting principle without judicially rewriting “the program” to mean only the Secretarial-amount-funded slice. Moreover, § 5325(m)(2)’s anti-offset rule, highlighted by Justice Sotomayor, reinforces the practical point: a Secretarial-amount-only CSC rule would effectively force tribes to subsidize federally required overhead tied to generating and deploying program income, undermining ISDEAA’s self-determination structure absent a clear statutory command. Ramah’s insistence (noted by Roberts and Gorsuch) that any narrowing be “clearly required” by the statutory language keeps me with Respondent because the government’s administrability concerns, while real, are not that clear command.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)–(3) defines contract support costs as the “reasonable costs” necessary to ensure compliance with the contract and prudent management of the “program,” and it does not textually limit those costs to activities financed only by the Secretarial amount. Where tribes use third‑party revenues to carry out and expand the very same contracted health program, the associated administrative and overhead burdens remain costs “required” to operate the contract program, and the Government has not shown that its narrower limitation is “clearly required by the statutory language,” as Ramah instructs in light of the ISDEAA’s liberal-construction/model-agreement principle. The Government’s appropriations and “open‑ended obligation” concerns are materially like the insufficient-funds arguments rejected in Ramah and Cherokee Nation, which held that the statutory scheme creates a binding obligation to pay full CSCs rather than prorating based on agency funding shortfalls. A narrow ruling can rest on the statutory text and Ramah’s interpretive framework without adopting broader theories about program income beyond recognizing that § 5325(m)(2) prevents third‑party revenues from being used to diminish the contract amount and does not supply a contrary cap on CSCs.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2)-(3) requires the Secretary to pay the “reasonable costs” necessary to ensure “contract compliance” and “prudent management” of the contracted health program, and it does not limit those support costs to activities funded only by the Secretarial amount. Because third-party reimbursements are expended to operate the same contracted program, the administrative and overhead costs required to manage that revenue and deliver the additional services remain “contract support costs” within the ordinary meaning of the statutory definition. Section 5325(m)(2) confirms that program income may not be used to reduce the amount the Secretary must provide, and nothing in the text converts that protection into a hidden cap on CSCs when tribes prudently use such income to run the contracted program. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, 567 U.S. 182 (2012), reinforces that where Congress has imposed a payment obligation in the ISDEAA, appropriations and agency allocation concerns do not justify rewriting the statute to pay less than the full, contractually required CSCs.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2)-(3) ties contract support costs to what is “required to ensure compliance with the terms of the contract” and to the operation of “the program” under the ISDEAA agreement, which is funded by the Secretarial amount; it does not clearly impose an additional federal payment obligation pegged to the tribe’s separate third-party revenue streams. Section 5325(m)(2) prevents program income from being used to reduce the Secretarial amount, but it does not affirmatively transform that income into a multiplier that expands CSC liability, and reading it that way risks an open-ended, self-amplifying obligation untethered to appropriations and administrability. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar required full payment of CSCs for the ISDEAA contract at issue, but it did not hold that CSCs must be recalculated on non-Secretarial funds (especially third-party collections) that a tribe chooses to expend, and we should not extend Ramah beyond its holding absent clear statutory command. Given the practical consequences for federal fiscal control and the absence of a clear textual directive for CSC-on-program-income, I would side with the government’s narrower reading.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)–(3) defines contract support costs as the “reasonable costs” necessary for contract compliance and prudent management of the contracted program, and it does not textually limit those costs to activities financed only by the Secretarial amount when the tribe is operating the same ISDEAA program with third‑party collections. Section 5325(m)(2) reinforces that program income is not to be used to reduce the federal contract amount, and reading it to foreclose corresponding CSC reimbursement would functionally shift federally required overhead onto tribes and undercut self-determination in precisely the way the Act was designed to prevent. Under Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, the government bears the burden to show its narrower reading is “clearly required by the statutory language,” and that showing is not met here given the Act’s liberal-construction directive (25 U.S.C. § 5329(c)) and the practical reality that third‑party revenue generates unavoidable administrative costs integral to running the contracted health program. Denying CSCs on those expenditures would predictably penalize tribes that successfully expand care through Medicaid/Medicare collections, harming access to healthcare for vulnerable populations Congress sought to protect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)-(3) defines CSCs as the reasonable costs necessary to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of the “contracted program,” and nothing in that text limits those costs to activities funded only by the Secretarial amount rather than the full operation of the contracted program as actually carried out. Section 5325(m)(2)’s rule that program income shall not be used to reduce the Secretarial amount fits comfortably with that reading: it prevents the Government from netting out third-party collections, but it does not create an unstated ceiling on what “contract support costs” may cover when those collections are used to run the same contracted program. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar underscores that the Government must pay CSCs in full as the statute specifies, and—given the ISDEAA’s liberal-construction directive in § 5329(c) and Ramah’s admonition that the Government must show its limitation is “clearly required”—the Government’s proposed Secretarial-amount-only restriction is not. Workability concerns about “open-ended” obligations are better addressed through the statute’s reasonableness requirement and ordinary contract/accounting controls, not by inserting a funding-source limitation Congress did not write.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2)-(3) requires the Secretary to pay the “reasonable costs for activities” needed to ensure “compliance with the terms of the contract” and “prudent management” of the “program,” and it does not limit those contract-support activities to the portion of program operations financed by the Secretarial amount. When a tribe uses third-party collections to operate the same contracted health program, the added administrative and compliance burdens remain “activities” necessary to carry out the contract and thus fall within the statute’s plain terms. Section 5325(m)(2) reinforces that “program income” is part of operating the program without reducing contract funding, and nothing in that provision supplies the limiting principle the government seeks. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar further instructs that, under the ISDEAA’s liberal-construction rule in § 5329(c), the government must show its narrower reading is “clearly required by the statutory language,” which it cannot do here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)-(3) defines contract support costs as the reasonable costs necessary to ensure compliance with the ISDEAA contract and prudent management of the “program,” and it does not textually limit those costs to activities funded only by the Secretarial amount. Section 5325(m)(2) reinforces that “program income” (including third-party reimbursements) is not to be used to reduce the contract amount, and reading the statute to deny CSCs on the administrative burden of operating the contracted program with that income would undercut the statutory structure and self-determination design. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar instructs that the Government must pay CSCs in full and, given the ISDEAA’s liberal-construction rule (25 U.S.C. § 5329(c)), the Government must show its narrowing limitation is clearly required by the statutory text—which it is not. Practical concerns about open-ended liability are for Congress to address through appropriations or amendments, not for the Court to supply by rewriting the CSC provisions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2) defines contract support costs as the “reasonable costs for activities” a tribe “must” carry on “as a contractor” to ensure contract compliance and prudent management, and nothing in that text limits those costs to work attributable only to the Secretarial amount rather than the operation of the contracted program as actually carried out. Section 5325(m)(2)’s rule that program income “shall not be a basis for reducing” contract funding cuts against importing an unstated ceiling that would effectively force tribes to absorb overhead generated by using third‑party collections to run the same contracted health programs. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar held that the Government must pay tribes’ CSCs “in full” when owed under the statutory formula, and the Government’s proposed limitation looks like the kind of atextual narrowing Ramah rejected in construing § 5325(a)(2)–(3). While appropriations constraints are relevant as a practical matter, the enacted text—read consistently with Ramah—ties CSCs to the reasonable support costs required to operate the contracted program, not merely to the subset of activities funded by the Secretarial amount.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)-(3) requires the Secretary to pay the “reasonable costs” necessary to ensure compliance with the ISDEAA contract and prudent management of the “program,” and it does not textually cap those support costs to activities financed solely by the Secretarial amount when the tribe is operating the same contracted healthcare program using third-party collections. Section 5325(m)(2) reinforces that program income (including third-party reimbursements) cannot be used to reduce contract funding, and reading the statute to deny CSCs for the administrative work required to generate and deploy that income would functionally shift mandatory overhead onto tribes and undermine self-determination in practical operation. Under Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, 567 U.S. 182 (2012), the Government’s underpayment of CSCs violates the statute and the contract, and ISDEAA’s pro-tribal interpretive direction (including the model agreement’s liberal-construction clause, see § 5329(c)) counsels against importing an extra-textual limitation that would predictably penalize tribes for effectively delivering care and securing reimbursements. While appropriations concerns are real, they cannot override the payment obligation Congress imposed for necessary contract support costs to run the contracted program as actually administered.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act requires the Indian Health Service to pay tribes additional “contract support costs” attributable to tribal health-program expenditures financed with the tribes’ own third‑party revenue (e.g., Medicare/Medicaid/insurance collections), beyond the amount of contract support costs associated with the federal “Secretarial amount.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA), primarily 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2)-(3) (definition and payment of “contract support costs”), with related provisions including § 5325(m)(2) (program income not a basis to reduce contract funds) and § 5329(c) (liberal construction/model agreement rule).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that ISDEAA’s contract-support-cost obligation is tied to the federal funds transferred under the self-determination contract (the “Secretarial amount”) and does not extend to additional administrative/overhead costs incurred because a tribe chooses to expand services using its own third‑party collections; reading the statute to require CSC on non-federal revenue would create an open-ended, potentially escalating federal liability that Congress did not clearly authorize, and other ISDEAA provisions (including the program-income rule) support the view that third-party revenue cannot increase the government’s payment obligation beyond the contract’s federal amount.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The tribes argue that the statutory definition of “contract support costs” covers the reasonable costs of activities necessary to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of the contracted health program, and that those costs are not limited to activities funded by the “Secretarial amount”; because third‑party collections are generated by operating the contracted program and are used to further that same program, the associated support/overhead is part of the CSC that ISDEAA obligates IHS to pay, and any ambiguity must be resolved in the tribes’ favor under ISDEAA’s liberal-construction directive and this Court’s CSC precedents.
key_precedents: Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, 567 U.S. 182 (2012)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s clear-statement/appropriations concern is the strongest point on the other side, but under my minimalist approach we cannot supply a Secretarial-amount cap that the enacted text does not contain: § 5325(a)(2)’s definition turns on the costs the Tribe “must” incur to ensure compliance and prudent management, and it is not facially source-of-funds dependent. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 5329(c) matters because it underscores that a narrowing construction must be “clearly required,” and I do not see that requirement met by policy fears about “potentially unlimited” liability. At the same time, to preserve administrability and institutional legitimacy, I would keep the holding narrow as Justice Kagan suggests: CSC are recoverable only insofar as they are reasonable, allowable, allocable, and non-duplicative under § 5325(a)(3)(A), which answers the parade of horribles without rewriting the statute. Cherokee Nation and Ramah, as Justice Barrett notes, reinforce that once the statute makes CSC part of the Government’s contractual obligation, courts should enforce it as written absent an express textual limitation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the appropriations/“unlimited liability” worry and his claim that CSC must be tethered to the Secretarial amount, but that limitation is not in the enacted text: § 5325(a)(2) defines CSC by the reasonable activities a tribe “must” perform to ensure compliance and prudent management of the contracted program, not by the provenance of the dollars spent. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 5325(m)(2) bars using program income as a basis to reduce amounts otherwise owed, and the government’s federal-dollars-only rule operates as just such a reduction when the tribe reinvests third-party revenues into the same contracted program. Ramah Navajo Chapter and Cherokee Nation (invoked by several colleagues) confirm we enforce these statutory payment obligations as written and do not graft budget-driven caps absent clear language, while § 5329(c) further requires any narrowing construction to be “clearly required,” which petitioner has not shown. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’ administrability point that the anti-duplication and “reasonable, allowable, allocable” limits do the textual work of preventing windfalls without inventing a Secretarial-amount cap.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s point that § 5325(a)(2) speaks in terms of costs the Tribe “must” incur, not the funding source, is the strongest textual pushback, but it still leaves unanswered what “funds otherwise obligated” are in § 5325(m)(2): I read that provision, as Justice Roberts notes, as barring offsets against the Government’s baseline obligation, not as converting every dollar of discretionary third-party program income into a trigger for additional federal CSC. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 5329(c) and Ramah/Cherokee Nation does not move the antecedent question; those cases enforce CSC “in full” once owed, but they do not hold that CSC are owed on expenditures attributable solely to non-federal expansions beyond the Secretarial amount the Government agreed to fund. I do not think the anti-duplication proviso alone answers the appropriations-sensitive structure here because the dispute is not duplication but the scope of what Congress made the United States pay for, and I see no clear textual hook for an open-ended escalator tied to third-party revenue. Under a textualist approach attentive to practical consequences, the narrower construction better fits the statutory bargain without reading § 5325(m)(2) as an affirmative ratchet.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s clear-statement/appropriations concern is the strongest point for petitioner, but it is ultimately a policy intuition looking for a textual hook: § 5325(a)(2)–(3) defines CSC by the reasonable costs a tribe “must” incur to ensure compliance and prudent management of the contracted program, not by whether a particular patient encounter was paid with federal appropriations or third-party revenue. As Justice Gorsuch and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, § 5329(c)’s liberal-construction rule means we cannot graft a “Secretarial-amount-only” cap unless it is “clearly required,” and the anti-duplication proviso in § 5325(a)(3)(A) is the statute’s chosen tool to prevent double recovery without denying necessary overhead. Justice Alito is right that § 5325(m)(2) is not an affirmative “escalator,” but denying CSC whenever tribes successfully collect and reinvest program income functions as the very reduction Congress prohibited, and in real-world terms it penalizes tribes for improving access to care. Cherokee Nation and Ramah, cited by multiple colleagues, reinforce that once the statute obligates payment, courts do not create budget-driven escape hatches absent clear limiting language.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is the appropriations/unlimited-liability concern and his premise that CSC must be tethered to the Secretarial amount, but the enacted definition in § 5325(a)(2)–(3) turns on “reasonable costs” the Tribe “must” incur to ensure compliance and prudent management of the contracted program, with the anti-duplication proviso as the express limiting mechanism—not a federal-dollars-only cap. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, reading § 5325(m)(2) as merely anti-offset still cuts against the Government here because denying CSC when tribes reinvest program income functions as a reduction of “funds otherwise obligated” for the same contracted program. Ramah and Cherokee Nation reinforce that courts should not invent budget-driven limitations on CSC obligations absent clear statutory text, and § 5329(c)’s liberal-construction rule makes Alito’s narrowing “Secretarial amount only” theory untenable unless it is clearly required. A pragmatic, workable boundary remains: CSC must be reasonable, allowable, allocable to operating the contracted program, and non-duplicative—addressing administrability without rewriting the statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s clear-statement/appropriations argument is the strongest pushback, but it asks us to graft a “Secretarial amount” cap onto § 5325(a)(2)’s definition of CSC—reasonable costs a Tribe “must” incur for compliance and prudent management—when Congress did not write that limitation. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, the better way to avoid the parade of horribles is to enforce the statute’s built-in constraints (reasonableness, allowability/allocability, and especially § 5325(a)(3)(A)’s anti-duplication rule), not invent a funding-source restriction. Alito’s reading of § 5325(m)(2) as merely anti-offset still runs into the fact that denying CSC whenever third-party program income is earned and reinvested functions as a reduction of “funds otherwise obligated” under the contract for the very same program. Ramah Navajo and Cherokee Nation, cited by Justices Thomas and Barrett, confirm that fiscal-exposure concerns cannot justify atextual limits on congressionally specified payment obligations absent language clearly requiring the narrowing construction (and § 5329(c) cuts against implying one).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the appropriations/“limitless liability” concern and the intuition that CSC must be pegged to the Secretarial amount, but that limitation is not in the operative text of § 5325(a)(2)–(3), which defines CSC by the reasonable costs the Tribe “must” incur to ensure compliance and prudent management of the contracted program—not by the revenue source for particular expenditures. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, we can address administrability and legitimacy concerns by holding narrowly that recoverable CSC must be reasonable, allowable, allocable to operating the contracted program, and non-duplicative under § 5325(a)(3)(A), without inventing a Secretarial-amount cap. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 5329(c)’s directive—that any narrowing construction must be “clearly required”—reinforces that fiscal-policy worries cannot supply an extra-textual limitation where Congress wrote a mandatory payment rule (“there shall be added”) and provided its own anti-duplication safeguard. Ramah and Cherokee Nation, as multiple colleagues note, confirm the institutional point: once Congress specifies a contract-payment obligation, we enforce it as written and leave budget fixes to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s clearest point is the appropriations/“limitless escalator” concern and his view that CSC must be tethered to the Secretarial amount, but that limitation is not in the text Congress enacted: § 5325(a)(2) defines CSC by the activities a tribe “must” undertake for compliance and prudent management of the contracted program, and § 5325(a)(3)(A) supplies the anti-duplication constraint rather than a source-of-funds cap. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan note, § 5325(m)(2)’s command that program income may not be used to “reduce the amount of funds otherwise obligated” is hard to reconcile with a construction that effectively denies otherwise-necessary CSC whenever third-party income is earned and reinvested in the same program. Ramah and Cherokee Nation (emphasized by Justices Thomas and Gorsuch) reinforce that absent a clear statutory cap, courts enforce the full CSC obligation as written; policy concerns about fiscal exposure cannot justify importing an extra-textual Secretarial-amount-only rule. I therefore remain with Respondent, with the holding cabined to reasonable, allowable, allocable, and non-duplicative CSC tied to operating the contracted program.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—the appropriations/“unlimited liability” concern—does not supply a legal basis to graft a “Secretarial-amount-only” cap onto § 5325(a)(2)–(3), which defines CSC by the reasonable costs the Tribe must incur to ensure compliance and prudent management of the contracted program as actually operated, regardless of the revenue stream paying particular line items. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 5325(m)(2) is not merely a passive anti-offset rule in practice here: denying CSC whenever third-party program income is earned and reinvested functions as a reduction in “funds otherwise obligated” for the same contracted program’s required administration. Ramah Navajo Chapter and Cherokee Nation reinforce that courts enforce these statutory contract obligations “in full” absent a limitation that is clearly required, and § 5329(c)’s liberal-construction rule makes it especially improper to resolve policy anxieties by importing extra-textual limits. Consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern, the limiting principles should come from the statute’s own guardrails—reasonableness, allowability, allocability, and the anti-duplication proviso—rather than a categorical funding-source restriction that Congress did not enact.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)-(3) defines “contract support costs” as the reasonable costs necessary to ensure compliance with, and prudent management of, the “contract,” and § 5325(m)(2) underscores that program income is part of operating the contracted program and cannot be used as a basis to reduce contract funding—making it difficult to treat third-party revenue as outside the contract’s cost structure when it is expended on the same contracted health program. Under § 5329(c)’s model-agreement liberal-construction rule, the Government must show its limiting construction (tying CSC strictly to the Secretarial amount) is “clearly required” by the statutory language, and that clarity is not apparent here. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar reinforces that CSC obligations are contractual and enforceable as written by Congress, and that interpretive doubts under ISDEAA are resolved in tribes’ favor absent a clear statutory limit. A narrow ruling can confine recovery to reasonable, allocable support costs attributable to expenditures on the contracted program (not an open-ended entitlement for unrelated tribal expansions), preserving institutional legitimacy while adhering to the statute’s text and structure.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2) requires payment of “contract support costs” for the reasonable costs of activities necessary “to ensure compliance with the terms of the contract and prudent management” of the contracted program, and it does not, by its terms, limit those costs to expenditures traceable solely to the “Secretarial amount.” Section 5325(m)(2) further provides that “program income” shall not be a basis to reduce contract amounts, which is most naturally read to prevent the Government from offsetting its CSC obligation when third-party revenue is generated in operating the federal program. Our precedents in Cherokee Nation v. Leavitt and Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar emphasize that ISDEAA contracts are binding obligations and that the Government must pay CSC “in full” as required by the statute, notwithstanding agency funding constraints. To the extent any ambiguity remains at the margins, § 5329(c)’s liberal-construction directive confirms reading the statute to cover CSC necessary to administer the contracted program as actually operated under the agreement, including when it is supplemented by third-party collections.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of ISDEAA ties the Government’s payment obligation to the federal amounts transferred under the self-determination contract—i.e., the “Secretarial amount”—and defines contract support costs as those “required by the Secretary” to carry out the contracted federal program, not an open-ended commitment to subsidize overhead generated by a tribe’s discretionary spending of non-federal third-party revenue. Reading § 5325(a)(2)-(3) to require additional CSC on expenditures financed with Medicare/Medicaid/insurance collections would create potentially unlimited, escalating federal liability without a clear statement from Congress, a result inconsistent with ordinary appropriations principles and practical consequences. Section 5325(m)(2)’s program-income rule prevents the Government from reducing contract funds because a tribe earns third-party revenue; it does not affirmatively obligate the Government to increase CSC payments beyond the contract’s federal funding. Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar required full payment of CSC owed under the contract’s federal funding and rejected pro rata payment based on agency shortfalls, but it did not compel CSC on costs attributable solely to non-federal expenditures outside the Secretarial amount.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: ISDEAA requires payment of “contract support costs” as the reasonable costs of activities the tribe “must” carry on to ensure compliance and prudent management of the contracted health program, 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2)-(3), and it also bars treating “program income” as a basis to reduce contract funds, § 5325(m)(2)—both provisions fit poorly with the Government’s attempt to cap CSC at the Secretarial amount when third-party collections are generated by and reinvested in the same contracted program. Under the Model Agreement’s liberal-construction rule, § 5329(c), the Government must show its narrower reading is “clearly required,” and Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar holds the Government must pay tribes’ CSC “in full” notwithstanding agency budgetary shortfalls, 567 U.S. 182, 194-95 (2012). Practically, denying CSC on third-party-funded expansions forces tribes to divert scarce health dollars to overhead, penalizing efficient revenue collection and undermining access to care for vulnerable patients the statute was designed to protect. If Congress wishes to limit this obligation, it can do so expressly; absent that clarity, the statute and precedent require payment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)-(3) requires IHS to add “contract support costs” that are the reasonable costs of activities necessary for contract compliance and prudent management of the “Federal program” carried out under the self-determination contract, and nothing in that text limits those necessary administrative costs to the subset attributable only to the Secretarial amount. Section 5325(m)(2) bars treating “program income” as a basis to reduce contract funds, which fits better with the tribes’ view that third-party collections used to operate the contracted program cannot be used to deny otherwise-necessary CSC, and § 5329(c)’s liberal-construction directive resolves any remaining ambiguity in favor of tribes. Our ISDEAA CSC cases emphasize that the Government must pay CSC in full when tribes incur them to run the contracted program and that underfunding is not a permissible budget-management device. Read as a coherent whole, the statute most naturally covers reasonable CSC generated by carrying out the contracted program even when the underlying service expansion is financed with third-party revenue.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The statute’s text requires that “[t]here shall be added to the amount required by paragraph (1) contract support costs,” defined as the “reasonable costs for activities which must be carried on … to ensure compliance with the terms of the contract and prudent management” of the contracted program, 25 U.S.C. § 5325(a)(2); that definition turns on what must be done to run the program the Tribe is contracting to operate, not on the revenue source used for particular expenditures. Section 5325(m)(2) reinforces that “program income” (including third-party collections) cannot be used “as a basis for reducing” contract amounts, undermining the government’s effort to treat third-party revenue as a limiting principle on CSC rather than as part of operating the same contracted program. Under § 5329(c)’s liberal-construction/model-agreement rule, and this Court’s instruction that the government must show its narrowing reading is “clearly required by the statutory language,” Salazar v. Ramah Navajo Chapter, 567 U.S. 182, 194 (2012), any residual ambiguity is resolved in the tribes’ favor. Separation-of-powers concerns about fiscal exposure cannot override Congress’s enacted text; if Congress wishes to cap CSC by reference to the Secretarial amount alone, it must do so clearly.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of ISDEAA § 5325(a)(2)–(3) requires payment of “contract support costs” for the reasonable and allowable costs necessary to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of the contracted program, and it contains no limitation tying CSC solely to activities funded by the “Secretarial amount,” apart from the anti-duplication proviso in § 5325(a)(3)(A). In Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, 567 U.S. 182 (2012), the Court read § 5325(a)(2)–(3) broadly and rejected the government’s attempt to cabin CSC to the Secretarial amount, emphasizing that Congress could have written such a limitation but did not. Section 5325(m)(2)’s rule that program income “shall not be a basis for reducing” contract funds does not, as Ramah explained, imply that program income cannot affect the amount of CSC owed; and § 5329(c)’s liberal-construction directive further supports resolving any residual ambiguity in the tribes’ favor. Given the statutory text and this Court’s established CSC precedents, the more workable and precedent-consistent reading is that IHS must pay CSC attributable to operating the contracted program, so long as there is no duplicative payment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2) directs that there “shall be added” to the Secretarial amount “contract support costs,” defined as the “reasonable costs for activities” a tribe “must” carry on “to ensure compliance with the terms of the contract and prudent management” of the contracted program, without a textual limitation to costs traceable only to federal dollars. Section 5325(m)(2) further provides that “program income” (including third-party collections) is not a basis to “reduce the amount of funds otherwise obligated to be paid” under the contract, which is more consistent with treating third-party revenue as part of operating the contracted program rather than as a cap on payable support costs. In Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, 567 U.S. 182 (2012), and Cherokee Nation v. Leavitt, 543 U.S. 631 (2005), the Court read ISDEAA to require payment of contract support costs in full when incurred under self-determination contracts, rejecting the Government’s underpayment theories absent clear statutory authorization. Any remaining ambiguity is reinforced in the tribes’ favor by ISDEAA’s liberal-construction directive, § 5329(c), which counsels against importing an extra-textual federal-funds-only limitation into § 5325(a)(2).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 5325(a)(2)-(3) defines “contract support costs” as the reasonable costs necessary to ensure contract compliance and prudent management of the contracted health program, and that definition does not, by its terms, cap CSC at the “Secretarial amount” when the tribe uses third-party revenue to carry out and expand the same contracted program. Section 5325(m)(2) reinforces that “program income” (including third-party collections) cannot be used as a basis to reduce contract funding, and reading the statute to deny CSC on program-funded expenditures would functionally penalize tribes for generating and reinvesting such income, undermining self-determination and producing perverse practical consequences. In Ramah Navajo Chapter v. Salazar, 567 U.S. 182 (2012), the Court required full payment of tribes’ reasonable CSC and emphasized that, under the model agreement’s liberal-construction rule codified at § 5329(c), the Government must show its limiting interpretation is “clearly required” by the statutory text—a showing it cannot make here given the broad CSC definition and Congress’s pro-tribal interpretive directive. Procedural fairness and equal-protection values embedded in the ISDEAA framework favor enforcing the statute as written so tribes are not forced to choose between expanding patient care with earned third-party funds and absorbing unfunded administrative burdens that the Act assigns to the United States.
